title: Collagen and myocyte interplay in cardiac volume overload: a multi-constituent growth and remodeling framework
authors: L. Maga; Mathias Peirlinck; L. Noël
abstract: Abstract Hearts subjected to volume overload (VO) are prone to detrimental anatomical and functional changes in response to elevated mechanical loading, ultimately leading to heart failure. Experimental findings now emphasize that organ-scale changes following VO cannot be explained by myocyte growth alone, as traditionally proposed in the literature. Collagen degradation, in particular, has been associated with VO and assumed to play a central role in both its acute and chronic stages. This hypothesis, however, remains to be substantiated by comprehensive mechanistic evidence, and each constituent contribution to myocardial growth and remodeling (G&R) processes is yet to be quantified. In this work, we present a multi-constituent G&R framework that integrates a mixture-based constitutive model within the kinematic growth formulation. This framework enables us to mechanistically assess the relative contributions of collagen and myocyte changes to alterations in tissue properties, ventricular dimensions, and growth phenotype. Our numerical results confirm that collagen remodeling affects the passive mechanical response of the myocardium, whereas myocytes predominantly influence the extent and phenotype of VO-induced growth. Importantly, collagen degradation exacerbates myocyte hypertrophy, revealing a synergistic interplay that accelerates the left ventricular eccentric growth and thereby promotes systolic dysfunction. This work constitutes an important step towards an integrated characterization of the early compensatory stages of VO-induced cardiac G&R.

title: Mitral regurgitation and left atrial phasic function and atrioventricular coupling in patients with myocardial infarction: a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging study
authors: Xiaoling Wen; Guo Ying-kun; Yue Gao; Zhi-Gang Yang
journal: Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery
abstract: Background: Mitral regurgitation (MR) after myocardial infarction (MI) may increase left atrial (LA) pressure and contribute to cardiac dysfunction. This study evaluated the incremental association of MR with LA phasic function and strain and identified independent factors associated with LA deformation in patients with MI. Methods: This retrospective study included 189 patients with MI (111 without MR and 78 with MR: mild, 27; moderate, 33; severe, 18) and 86 normal controls who underwent 3.0-T cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). MR severity was graded by the CMR-derived MR fraction: mild <30%, moderate 30% to <50%, and severe ≥50%. CMR-derived LA phasic function and strain (reservoir strain, epsilon-s; booster strain, epsilon-a; conduit strain, epsilon-e), left ventricular (LV) function and strain, infarct size, and MR fraction were measured. Between-group comparisons were performed using one-way analysis of variance or the Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc correction, and multivariable linear regression was used to identify independent factors associated with LA strain. A two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Patients with MI and MR had lower LA reservoir strains [22.14%±10.91% vs. 28.65% (22.78%, 38.30%) vs. 41.70% (36.15%, 53.15%)], booster strains [11.52%±6.19% vs. 13.80% (10.20%, 19.80%) vs. 19.25% (15.10%, 24.05%)], and conduit strains [9.40% (6.03%, 14.85%) vs. 14.60% (9.60%, 20.50%) vs. 22.55% (17.75%, 30.43%)] than patients with MI without MR and controls (all P<0.05). They also had higher LA maximum volume [68.43 (57.44, 91.51) mL] and minimum volume [35.93 (24.43, 61.15) mL] and lower LA total ejection fraction (45.39%±14.97%) than the other groups (all P<0.05). In multivariable analysis, MR degree was independently associated with reservoir strain (β=−0.194, P=0.048) and conduit strain (β=−0.208, P=0.038). Anterior wall MI (reservoir strain: β=−0.245, P=0.014; booster strain: β=−0.231, P=0.028; conduit strain: β=−0.224, P=0.027) and posteromedial papillary muscle infarction (reservoir strain: β=−0.329, P=0.004; booster strain: β=−0.370, P=0.003) were also independently associated with LA strain. Conclusions: MR was associated with further deterioration of LA myocardial strain in patients with MI. Posteromedial papillary muscle infarction, anterior wall MI, beta-blocker use, and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel were independently associated with LA strain. CMR-derived functional and strain parameters may help characterize LV-LA coupling and support risk stratification in this population.

title: Advantages and Limitations of the Use of Robots in Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair: Results From a Matched Direct Comparison
authors: Kosuke Nakamae; Yoshitsugu Nakamura; Daiki Yoshiyama; Yuto Yasumoto; Miho Kuroda; Shintaro Sawa; Yuka Higuma; Kusumi Niitsuma; Masaki Ushijima; Akihiro Higashino; Yujiro Hayashi; Taisuke Nakayama; Hiroaki Yusa; Ryo Tsuruta; Yujiro Ito
journal: Innovations Technology and Techniques in Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery
abstract: Objective: To compare the surgical outcomes of nonrobotic and robotic minimally invasive mitral valve repair. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair from January 2014 to March 2024. After excluding the learning curve cases, early and midterm outcomes were compared. Results: A total of 422 patients who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair (nonrobotic, n = 103; robotic, n = 319) were enrolled. The robotic group had a higher EuroSCORE II ( P < 0.001). After propensity matching, the final cohort included 84 and 168 patients in each group. In the robotic group after matching, concomitant procedures remained significantly more frequent ( P = 0.030). However, operative time ( P = 0.782) and cross-clamping time ( P = 0.452) were comparable, whereas cardiopulmonary bypass time was significantly longer in the robotic group ( P = 0.031). Postoperative blood transfusion ( P < 0.001), chest tube output within 24 h ( P < 0.001), and intensive care unit stay ( P = 0.042) remained higher in the robotic group after matching. Postoperative mitral regurgitation was no greater than mild in both groups ( P = 0.146). At 4 years, overall survival was 94.4% versus 98.4% ( P = 0.215), and freedom from recurrence of moderate or greater mitral regurgitation was 98.5% versus 97.9% ( P = 0.230) after matching. These results are consistent with those observed before matching. Conclusions: Robotic mitral valve repair demonstrated comparable perioperative and midterm outcomes despite greater transfusion requirements and a higher frequency of concomitant procedures. The higher rate of concomitant procedures should be interpreted with caution because it may partly reflect differences in surgical era and patient selection.

title: Exercise Echocardiography in the Diagnostic Work-up of Unexplained Dyspnoea: A Critical Narrative Review of Physiological Targets, Diagnostic Performance and Unresolved Controversies
authors: Malki Mohamed; Loudiyi Nadia; Lakhal Zouhair; Benyass Aatif
journal: Asian Journal of Research in Medical and Pharmaceutical Sciences
abstract: Background: Chronic exertional dyspnoea frequently remains unexplained after clinical assessment, natriuretic peptide measurement and resting echocardiography. Many underlying cardiovascular abnormalities, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and exercise pulmonary hypertension, become apparent only during physiological stress. Exercise echocardiography is non-invasive, widely available and free of ionising radiation, but its diagnostic role outside ischaemia testing remains contested. Purpose and Scope: This critical narrative review evaluates the evidence supporting exercise echocardiography in adults with chronic exertional dyspnoea that remains unexplained after first-line evaluation. It examines test conduct and feasibility, the diastolic stress test, pulmonary vascular and right ventricular responses, ischaemic, valvular and dynamic obstructive causes, and multiparametric approaches incorporating lung ultrasound, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and artificial intelligence. Methods: Literature was identified through structured searches of bibliographic databases and scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and professional-society guidance. Evidence was appraised with attention to patient spectrum, reference standards, feasibility reporting and outcome relevance, and synthesised thematically. Principal Findings: Invasive studies consistently show that exercise unmasks haemodynamic abnormalities that resting tests miss. Exercise-derived echocardiographic abnormalities, including elevated filling-pressure surrogates, exercise pulmonary hypertension and exercise-induced pulmonary congestion, carry consistent prognostic information. The diagnostic accuracy of individual markers, especially the ratio of early mitral inflow to early diastolic annular velocity, is considerably less secure: validation studies conflict, largely because of differences in patient spectrum, reference standards and measurement timing. Tricuspid regurgitation signals are frequently unobtainable at peak exercise, and the incremental value of stress testing over probability scores appears modest in several invasive validation cohorts. Left atrial mechanics, systolic reserve, cardiac output-indexed pulmonary pressures and lung ultrasound show promise but require external validation. Unresolved Questions: Consensus is lacking on the reference standard, age- and sex-specific normal responses, optimal protocols and the effect of test-guided management on patient outcomes. Implications and Conclusion: Exercise echocardiography is best regarded as a question-driven, multiparametric physiological test integrated with pre-test probability and, where available, gas-exchange measurement, rather than as a single-parameter rule-in or rule-out tool. Prospective multicentre studies with invasive reference standards and outcome-oriented diagnostic trials are needed before stronger recommendations can be justified.

title: PASCAL Precision System Outcomes by Implant Location and Lesion Location in Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation Patients From the STS/ACC TVT Registry
authors: P. Kasi Ramanathan; Raj Makkar; Thomas E. Waggoner; Azeem Latib; Robert Kipperman; Ivan Hanson; Anjan Sinha; Tarun Chakravarty; Rahul P. Sharma; Jeremiah Peter Depta; Jorge Castellanos; Susheel Kodali; Amar Krishnaswamy; Brian K. Whisenant; Daniel S. Menees; David Scott Lim; Fahad Syed Gilani; Carlos E. Sanchez; Neil M. Gheewala; Santiago A. Garcia; Hemal Gada; Samir Ramesh Kapadia; Pinak Bipin Shah; Brian M. Renard; Gus Theodos; Ricardo Yaryura; Blake Gardner; Daniel Howard Steinberg; Eric Gnall; Georges Kaddissi; Adnan K. Chhatriwalla; Antonio Halais Frangieh; Mackram F. Eleid; Philippe Généreux; John Thomas Saxon; Pedro Arturo Villablanca; Fadi Matar; Himanshu Agarwal; Stan J. Chetcuti; Tiberio Frisoli; Firas E. Zahr
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background Mitral valve transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair can be more challenging in noncentral regions of the valve and in anterior or bileaflet lesions. We assess effect of implant location and leaflet lesion location on safety and effectiveness of PASCAL Precision system in degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR). Methods Mitral valve transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair outcomes in patients with degenerative MR treated with PASCAL Precision system (September 2022–October 2024), from the US STS/ACC TVT (Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapy) Registry, were analyzed by implant location (A2P2/non‐A2P2) and leaflet lesion location (anterior/posterior/bileaflet). Procedural, clinical, and echocardiographic outcomes to 30 days were assessed. Results At 30 days, both A2P2 (n=1526) and non‐A2P2 (n=299) groups had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 1.1% versus 1.0%, mitral valve reintervention: 0.4% versus 0.0% and single leaflet device attachment: 0.5% versus 0.3%; all P >0.05) and demonstrated significant MR reduction ( P <0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference between groups ( P =0.750) (MR ≤2+: 93.4% versus 95.4%; MR ≤1+: 72.0% versus 73.3%). Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores improved significantly in both groups (∆19.3, ∆17.7 points; P =0.741). The anterior (n=250), posterior (n=902), and bileaflet (n=192) disease groups also had low event rates (cardiovascular mortality: 0.4%, 1.1%, 0.0%; mitral valve reintervention: 0.8%, 0.1%, 0.5%; and single leaflet device attachment: 0.8%, 0.2%, 0.5%; all P >0.05), and demonstrated significant MR reduction ( P <0.001 versus baseline) with no significant difference across groups ( P =0.459) (MR ≤2+: 94.1%, 93.1%, and 94.5%; MR ≤1+: 79.0%, 69.2%, and 72.4%). All groups experienced significant improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary scores (∆21.4, ∆18.8, ∆12.0 points; P =0.087). Conclusion In real‐world patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation, treatment with the PASCAL Precision system was associated with favorable safety and effectiveness at 30 days, regardless of implant location or leaflet lesion location.

title: The predictive value of the hemodynamic profile for survival in patients undergoing transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair
authors: Felix Ausbuettel; Fares Kano; Nikolaos Patsalis; Christin Fichera; Dimitar Divchev; Carlo-Federico Fichera
abstract: Transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (M-TEER) represents a safe treatment modality for patients with high-grade mitral regurgitation (MR). While clinical decision-making concerning the referral of suitable candidates for M-TEER is guided primarily by clinical and echocardiographic parameters, the potential of hemodynamic parameters obtained at the time of screening in predicting treatment outcomes has not been sufficiently investigated. All patients who underwent M-TEER and who provided sufficient right heart catheterisation (RHC) data prior to M-TEER were enrolled for analysis. The investigated hemodynamic parameters were analysed descriptively and their associations with survival were estimated by univariable Cox regression analysis and Kaplan–Meier’s analysis. A total of 94 patients were analysed, of whom 92.6% (87/94) had concomitant pulmonary hypertension (PH). Analysis of the hemodynamic profile revealed that 46.8% (44/94) of patients had advanced-stage congestive heart failure with a cardiac index < 2 L/min/m2, and 68% (64/94) of patients had a cardiac power index <0.5 W/m2. According to the results of the Kaplan–Meier and Cox regression analyses, a systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) > 60 mmHg and a mean right atrial pressure (RAP) > 20 mmHg were proven to be significant predictors of long-term survival after M-TEER. Analysis of the hemodynamic profile, specifically the identified predictors, contributes to the improved identification of scenarios associated with a favourable prognosis in patients undergoing M-TEER. CI: cardiac index; CPI: cardiac power index; meanRAP: mean right atrial pressure; M-TEER: transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair; PH: pulmonary hypertension; RHC: right heart catheterisation; sPAP: systolic pulmonary artery pressure.

title: Evaluation of echocardiographic abnormalities and associated factors in 100 hemodialysis patients
authors: Hakimeh Saadatifar; Khojasteh Marashi; Zahra Eslamifar; Saber Rostami; Aziz Kasani; Soraya Khajehrezaei
abstract: Abstract Background Systematic assessment of cardiac remodeling in hemodialysis (HD) patients is essential for cardiovascular risk stratification. Echocardiography is a widely available tool for evaluating structural and functional cardiac abnormalities. We investigated associations between clinical and dialysis-related parameters and echocardiographic abnormalities among patients receiving chronic HD at the Dezful Nephrology Center in southwestern Iran. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 160 adults undergoing chronic HD were screened and 100 met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. All participants underwent transthoracic echocardiography. Associations between echocardiographic abnormalities and age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, body mass index (BMI), dyslipidemia, coronary and non-coronary vascular disease, dialysis access type, dialysis vintage, anemia, plasma lipid concentrations, and resting heart rate were evaluated Bivariate analyses were followed by multivariable logistic regression for prespecified binary echocardiographic outcomes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. A two-sided P -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Echocardiographic abnormalities were present in 86% of patients. After multivariable adjustment, hypertension (aOR 2.80, 95% CI 1.30–6.00), coronary artery disease (aOR 6.10, 95% CI 1.90–19.60), non-coronary vascular disease (aOR 4.20, 95% CI 1.30–13.60), and lower plasma triglycerides (aOR 0.99 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98–0.995) were independently associated with left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Diabetes was associated with diastolic dysfunction (aOR 2.60, 95% CI 1.10–6.20) and moderate-to-severe mitral or tricuspid regurgitation (aOR 2.40, 95% CI 1.00–5.70). Dialysis access type and non-coronary vascular disease were linked to left ventricular hypertrophy. Lower plasma triglycerides, higher resting heart rate, and non-coronary vascular disease were associated with right ventricular abnormality. Lower BMI and lower plasma triglycerides were associated with a higher aortic index. Traditional risk factors together with dialysis-related parameters, particularly low serum triglycerides, low BMI, and arteriovenous fistula access, showed independent associations with specific echocardiographic phenotypes. Conclusion Echocardiographic abnormalities are highly prevalent in this HD cohort and independently associated with both traditional cardiovascular risk factors and selected dialysis-related parameters, including low plasma triglycerides, low BMI, and the presence of arteriovenous fistula. These findings support closer clinical attention to these variables for cardiac risk stratification in hemodialysis patients. Given the cross-sectional design and modest sample size, the results represent associations rather than causal effects. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Management Anesthesia of Lumbar Plexus Block and Sacral Plexus Block for Hip Disarticulation Due to ALI Rutherford IIB with Severe Cardiac and Pulmonary Problems
authors: Akhiruddin Akhiruddin; Akhmad Yun Jufan; Farhan Ali; Ratih Kumala Fajar Apsari
journal: Solo Journal of Anesthesi Pain & Critical Care (SOJA)
abstract: Background : Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency associated with a high risk for limb loss and death. Peripheral artery disease is responsible for 12 to 15% of deaths in Europe. The spectrum ranges from asymptomatic or intermittent claudication to necrosis and limb loss2. Case Illustration : A 68 year old man with a diagnosis of Rutherford IIB acute limb ischemia (ALI) in the left leg presented with complaints of blackening extending to the upper lower extremity. The patient was admitted to the cardiac HCU with a diagnosis of low EF 24%, severe segmental kinetic disorder, LV apical thrombus, LV sec, grade 3 pulmonary edema, pulmonary consolidation sinistra, pneumonia dextra and sepsis. The patient was scheduled for left hip disarticulation. Anesthesia management involved a lumbar plexus block with isobaric bupivacaine 0.5% 20 mL (100 mg) and a sacral plexus block with isobaric bupivacaine 0.5% 15 mL (75 mg). After the hip disarticulation procedure, the patient desaturation until 88%, suplementation oksigen with non rebreathing mask (NRM) at 15 lpm, improving to 95%. The patient was admitted to the ICU. In the ICU, the saturation was 90% with NRM at 15 lpm, so non invasive ventilation (NIV) was used with a pressure support of 5, PEEP of 5 and FiO2 of 100%. The patient also hypoglycemia (23 g/dl). After evaluation with GDS and weaning off NIV, the patient was transferred to the ward with a Numeric Rating Score (NRS) of 1-2. Conclusion : The operation lasted for 3 hours with no pain during the procedure and stable vital signs monitoring. Pain evaluation after the operation showed a score of 1-2 using the Numeric Rating Score (NRS).

title: Tricuspid regurgitation after left-sided STEMI: an independent marker of adverse prognosis
authors: Dmitri Guz; Leor Perl; Yaron Shapira; Katia Orvin; Tamir Bental; Ran Kornowski; Mordehay Vaturi
abstract: Risk stratification for patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) primarily focuses on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and ischemic mitral regurgitation (MR), whereas the prognostic significance of tricuspid regurgitation (TR) after left-sided STEMI remains poorly defined. We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients presenting with a first LAD- or LCX-related STEMI between 2000 and 2019 who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Patients with prior myocardial infarction, revascularization, or significant valvular disease were excluded. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed within 24 h of PCI. Significant TR was defined as at least moderate regurgitation. The primary endpoint was long-term all-cause mortality. Among 1,273 patients with left-sided STEMI, moderate or severe TR was present in 74 patients (5.8%). Patients with significant TR had higher all-cause mortality (44.6% vs. 10.8%; p < 0.001), in-hospital mortality (12.2% vs. 1.9%; p < 0.001), and 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (39.2% vs. 15.3%; p < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower long-term survival among patients with significant TR (log-rank p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, comorbidities, infarct size, LVEF, MR, and right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), TR remained independently associated with mortality (HR 2.84, 95% CI 1.43–5.6; p = 0.002). Propensity score-matched analysis confirmed these findings. Importantly, TR remained associated with higher long-term all-cause mortality even among patients with preserved LVEF (27.3% vs. 3.7%; p = 0.011). Moderate or greater TR after left-sided STEMI is independently associated with adverse outcomes beyond those attributable to reduced LVEF and MR. Not applicable.

title: Complex Airway Management in Pierre Robin Sequence with Failed Intubation: Case Report and Lesson Learned
authors: Ade Novita; Ricky Aditya
journal: Solo Journal of Anesthesi Pain & Critical Care (SOJA)
abstract: Background : Pierre Robin Sequence (PRS) is a rare condition with a global prevalence of 1 in 8,500-14,000 live births, characterized by micrognatia, glossoptosis, and upper airway obstruction. Reporting this case is essential to enriching the literature on PRS management, especially in Indonesia, where case data is still limited. Case Illustration : A 1 year ten months old child with PRS, palatoschizis, laryngomalacia, secondary hypothyroidism, and mandibular hypoplasia. The patient will undergo mandibular osteodistraction to address airway obstruction and improve facial structure. Since birth, the patient has shown feeding difficulties and airway obstruction. At five months of age, an echocardiography examination revealed a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The patient was fasted for 6 hours before surgery, intravenous access was established, and premedication with midazolam 0.05mg/kgBB. Preoxygenation, induction with ketamine 1mg/kgBB, intubation with spiral ETT No. 3.5 and atracurium 0,5mg/kgBB were given, and maintenance anaesthesia using sevoflurane. Close monitoring was done to ensure the patient's stability. Postoperatively, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit with intravenous paracetamol analgesic and close monitoring to prevent complications. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of meticulous airway planning in children with Pierre Robin Sequence (PRS) and a history of failed intubation. Successful anaesthetic management was achieved through preoperative airway assessment, adequate preoxygenation, successful tracheal intubation before administration of neuromuscular blockade, and maintenance with sevoflurane. Given the potential for difficult ventilation and intubation in PRS, appropriate preparation for advanced airway techniques and multidisciplinary collaboration are essential.

title: Blood Culture-negative Infective Endocarditis with Fatal Ischaemic Hepatitis in a Patient on Antitubercular Therapy: A Case Report
authors: Mittal Sindhav; Ronak Shah; Parth Shah
journal: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC RESEARCH
abstract: Infective Endocarditis (IE) in patients receiving Antitubercular Therapy (ATT) is easily missed, because rifampicin can sterilise blood cultures and blunt the febrile and inflammatory response, delaying recognition until multiorgan failure is already established. The present case report is of a 45-year-old male in the fourth month of HRZE (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) ATT for pulmonary tuberculosis who presented afebrile with a two-day history of dyspnoea and haemodynamic collapse. Emergency physician bedside Point-Of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS) showed a collapsible Inferior Vena Cava (IVC), an ejection fraction of 35%, a thickened calcified aortic valve with a mobile vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation, and moderate functional mitral regurgitation. Initial Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) showed pH 7.19 and lactate 15 mmol/L; over the next five hours the acidosis worsened (pH 7.12) although lactate was 12.8 mmol/L, despite initial supportive measures. Following IVC-guided fluid resuscitation, vasopressor optimisation, and Intermittent Haemodialysis (IHD) from day 3, lactate improved to a nadir of 5.1 mmol/L on day 3 before re-rising to 8.9 mmol/L by day 5, paralleling progressive multiorgan failure. Serum Glutamic-Oxaloacetic Transaminase (SGOT) was 7,279 IU/L (182 times the upper limit of normal) at presentation, indicating pre-arrival ischaemic hepatitis, and exceeded 20,000 IU/L by day 2. Two pre-antibiotic blood culture sets remained negative for growth at 96 hours (Day 4) of incubation, consistent with probable rifampicin-associated blood culture-negative endocarditis. The patient died on day 5 after a cardiac arrest unresponsive to resuscitation. This case demonstrates that IE on a tuberculosis-predisposed calcified valve can present afebrile with extreme hyperlactataemia and established ischaemic hepatitis, and that an early lactate-clearance response does not preclude terminal re-deterioration once hepatic and multiorgan failure are structurally established.

title: Perioperative anaesthetic management of EHPVO with coexisting severe valvular and congenital heart disease
authors: Shilpa Sarang Kore; Pritish Vijh
abstract: Background: Anaesthetic management of extrahepatic portal venous obstruction (EHPVO) is chal-lenging when associated with congenital heart disease, severe mitral regurgitation (MR), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The competing haemodynamic re-quirements and risk of variceal bleeding require careful perioperative planning.Case Presetation: A 47-year-old woman with EHPVO and portal hypertension was scheduled for oesoph-agogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic variceal ligation and oesophageal dilatation under general anaesthesia. She had congenital conductive hearing loss, mutism, right eye blindness, and a partial atrioventricular septal defect with an ostium primum atri-al septal defect and persistent left-to-right shunt. Echocardiography showed a cleft mi-tral valve with severe MR, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, moderate PAH, and pre-served biventricular function. Preoperative investigations revealed anaemia, spleno-megaly, and oesophageal varices. General anaesthesia was administered with invasive arterial and central venous pressure monitoring. Induction with midazolam, fentanyl, and etomidate was followed by rocuronium. Controlled ventilation was used to main-tain oxygenation and normocapnia and avoid increases in pulmonary vascular re-sistance. Meticulous de-airing of intravenous lines was performed. The procedure was completed successfully without significant haemodynamic instability or bleeding. Neu-romuscular blockade was reversed with sugammadex, followed by uneventful extuba-tion. The patient remained stable during 24 hours of postoperative ICU monitoring.Conclusion: Patients with EHPVO and complex cardiac disease require individualized anaesthetic management, with emphasis on haemodynamic stability, avoidance of increased pulmonary vascular resistance, careful fluid administration, airway protection, and vigilant postoperative monitoring.

title: Update in short-term mechanical circulatory support: indications, devices and complications
authors: José María Moreno-Coca; E Moreno-Monterde; A Manzano; Rut Andrea; Marc Giménez‐Milà
abstract: Despite advances in early recognition, aetiology-directed therapy, intensive cardiovascular care and short-term mechanical circulatory support (MCS), cardiogenic shock (CS) remains associated with high mortality and morbidity. MCS can restore systemic perfusion and stabilise patients as a bridge to recovery or advanced heart failure therapies, or as a bridge-to-decision when the final therapeutic destination remains uncertain. However, appropriate patient and device selection remains challenging. The optimal timing of support is uncertain, as both premature implantation and delayed use in advanced shock may limit benefit while increasing complications. Device selection should therefore be individualised according to the predominant patient phenotype, including left ventricular, right ventricular or biventricular failure, concomitant respiratory failure, vascular access and anatomical considerations. Randomised trials have focused predominantly on acute myocardial infarction-related CS, whereas data in heart failure-related and acute-on-chronic CS remain limited. Recent trials have also shown that greater haemodynamic support does not uniformly translate into improved survival, highlighting the importance of matching device physiology to shock phenotype and clinical trajectory. MCS is associated with clinically relevant complications, including major bleeding, haemolysis, limb ischaemia, stroke, thrombosis and vascular injury. Accordingly, its use should be considered within a strategy integrating reversibility, neurological prognosis, recovery potential, a realistic definitive therapeutic strategy, technical feasibility and anticipated complication risk. This Mini Review summarises contemporary indications, devices and complications of MCS in CS, with emphasis on phenotype-guided selection, timing, intensive care management and current evidence gaps.

title: Pacing during TAVR through a coronary wire in the coronary artery and left ventricular wire
authors: Ruisong Ma; Lili Zhang; Wang Liao; Sheng Wang
abstract: The conventional pacing-over-the-wire technique in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) results in high impedance and voltage thresholds, which may cause loss of capture and valve embolisation. Our team reported that coronary wire pacing, in which a coronary wire is placed in the left coronary artery (anode) and a left ventricular wire (cathode), is associated with extremely low impedance and pacing voltage thresholds in patients who are at high risk of coronary obstruction. Moreover, coronary wire pacing is simple and reliable. In this study, we illustrate the coronary wire pacing technique in a patient to provide a new approach to wire pacing in TAVR.

title: Troponin I and CPK-MB in Chronic Kidney Disease Stage IV and V
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, particularly coronary artery disease (CAD).Interpretation of cardiac biomarkers in CKD is challenging because reduced renal clearance may result in elevated baseline levels.This study evaluated the utility of Troponin I (Trop I) and Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB) in detecting CAD among patients with CKD Stage IV and V. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in the Departments of General Medicine, Cardiology, and Nephrology at Vydehi Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre from March 2023 to August 2024.Ninety patients aged >18 years with CKD Stage IV or V were enrolled.Demographic details, clinical history, laboratory investigations, serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), Troponin I, CK-MB, electrocardiography, and two-dimensional echocardiography findings were recorded.Comparisons were made between patients with and without CAD.Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic performance of Troponin I. Results:The mean age of participants was 58.93 ± 12.00 years, and 71.1% were males.CAD was present in 28 (31.1%)patients.Serum creatinine and eGFR were comparable between CAD and non-CAD groups (p>0.05).Mean Troponin I levels were significantly higher in patients with CAD than those without CAD (1.10 ± 1.18 vs. 0.04 ± 0.05 ng/mL; p<0.001).In contrast, CK-MB levels did not differ significantly between groups (4.71 ± 6.47 vs. 3.73 ± 3.44 ng/mL; p=0.352).ROC analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance of Troponin I for predicting CAD, with an AUC of 0.946, sensitivity of 89.29%, specificity of 98.39%, and an optimal cut-off value of >0.15 ng/mL.Conclusion: Troponin I is a reliable and clinically useful biomarker for detecting CAD in patients with CKD Stage IV and V, whereas CK-MB has limited diagnostic value.Troponin I may aid cardiovascular risk stratification when interpreted alongside clinical and imaging findings.

title: Pre-existing cardiovascular disease and critical illness recovery: A multi-method study of the impact and experiences of patients and relatives
authors: Nicola Mary Anne Rea
journal: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: Background: Approximately 25% of critically ill patients have pre-existing CVD. Research has shown that pre-critical illness health and the presence of co-morbidities are linked to adverse outcomes. Yet, little is known about the impact of pre-existing CVD or how it is managed during critical illness recovery. Aim: To explore the role of pre-existing CVD in determining recovery outcomes, experiences, and support needs beyond the hospital setting for critical illness survivors and their relatives. Methods: This thesis adopted a pragmatic multi-method approach comprising three studies. First, a systematic review explored experiences and perspectives of physical symptoms in the context of follow-up care. It employed a reflexive thematic analysis approach. Second, a retrospective observational cohort study investigated the impact of pre-existing CVD on emergency critical care survivors. A binary logistic regression using multiple imputation was run with one-year hospital readmission as the primary outcome. Third, a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews explored the perspectives of critical illness survivors with pre-existing CVD and their relatives on experiences of recovery and support. Findings: The systematic review (n=11) highlighted that baseline health influences how patients perceive recovery, and that follow-up care often fails to address pre-existing co-morbidities. The quantitative study (n=51,625) found pre-existing CVD was prevalent (17.1%) and is associated with higher hospital readmission rates (OR 1.20). The qualitative study (n=12) identified Post-Intensive Care Syndrome is the dominant factor in short-term recovery rather than pre-existing CVD. Further, it emphasised the need for active involvement of patients and relatives in care. Conclusion: Pre-existing CVD may be clinically relevant, yet from a patient perspective, priorities and support are misaligned. Further, current healthcare service delivery does not adequately account for the importance of pre-existing CVD during critical illness recovery. This thesis has shown that pre-existing CVD may be associated with adverse outcomes and highlights a gap in care.

title: Remote monitoring in patients awaiting elective cardiac surgery is associated with improved clinical outcomes: a prospective service evaluation
authors: Arun Kirupananthavel; Martin T. Yates; Kulvinder S. Lall; Simon Woldman; Shivani Joshi; Nimra Ahsan; Adem Aktas; Gordon Ferguson; Nay Aung; Charles J. Knight; Andrew Wragg; Debashish Das; Stephen Edmondson
abstract: Abstract Background Rising elective cardiac surgery waiting times are associated with increased risk of clinical deterioration and unscheduled admissions. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) may offer earlier detection of deterioration, but its role during the pre-operative waiting period is not well established. Methods We conducted a prospective single centre service evaluation of a digital RPM pathway for adults listed for elective cardiac surgery between September 2022 and September 2023. Patients submitting at least one digital symptom questionnaire (activated group) were compared with those who did not (non-activated). Primary outcomes were preoperative mortality and unscheduled admissions requiring non elective intervention. Secondary outcomes included resternotomy, 1 year postoperative mortality, and length of stay. Results Of 1,164 patients, 799 (68.6%) were activated. Baseline characteristics were similar aside from higher hypertension and diabetes prevalence in the non-activated group. Pre-operative mortality was significantly lower in activated patients (0.6% vs 2.2%; RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09–0.87; p=0.018). Unscheduled admissions were also reduced (2.1% vs 4.3%; RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.95; p=0.031). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated early and sustained separation (log-rank p=0.012). Secondary outcomes were similar between groups. In the propensity-matched cohort, activation remained associated with lower pre-operative mortality (0.7% vs 3.5%; RR 0.20; p=0.027) and fewer unscheduled admissions (2.0% vs 5.8%; RR 0.35; p=0.026). Conclusion Implementation of a structured pre-operative RPM pathway was feasible at scale and associated with significantly reduced pre-operative mortality and fewer unplanned admissions. These findings support RPM as a promising strategy to enhance safety and stability for patients awaiting elective cardiac surgery.

title: Dietary acrylamide and AGE products in processed pet food: a review of the evidence and implications for safety thresholds in dogs and cats
authors: Andreas Hopf; Matthew Muir; Alex England; Fariba Dehghani
abstract: Traditionally processed pet foods, including kibble (dry), and retorted or canned formats (wet), are manufactured using high-temperature thermal processing methods that drive the formation of Maillard reaction products (MRPs) and acrylamide (AA). Dogs and cats commonly consume the same traditionally processed food as a daily dietary staple over prolonged periods, resulting in chronic, sustained dietary exposure to these compounds. In humans and rodents, dietary advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and AA are associated with diabetes, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and forms of cancer through mechanisms including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, protein cross-linking, and activation of the receptor for advanced glycation end-products (RAGE). Dietary restriction of these compounds reduces disease markers in humans and rodents. Studies in companion animals indicate that dietary AGE intake influences systemic AGE exposure, and that mildly processed diets are linked to lower circulating AGE concentrations. Adverse health outcomes attributable to these compounds have not been demonstrated in companion animals. Unlike for human food, no regulatory benchmarks for acrylamide exist in pet foods, and no benchmarks for AGEs exist in any jurisdiction. This review examines the evidence on dietary AGEs and AA and health outcomes in humans and rodents, considers its potential relevance to companion animals, and discusses mildly processed diets as an alternative approach worth investigating.

title: Admission high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T and clinical outcomes after acute ischemic stroke: a retrospective cohort study with exploratory nonlinear analysis
authors: Yisheng Chen; Suhua Liu; Hua Xue; Rui Wang; Rongfang Wen; 肖兆祥; Xuerong Sheng; Peifeng Chen; Na Song; Yongkun Li
abstract: Background Elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) is frequently observed in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and has been associated with adverse outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the association of admission hs-cTnT with 90-day functional outcome and all-cause mortality during follow-up, with particular attention to potential nonlinear risk patterns across the biomarker range. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included 564 patients with AIS admitted between January 2022 and October 2024. The primary outcomes were modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 90 days and long-term all-cause mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used for poor 90-day functional outcome and Cox proportional hazards models were used for all-cause mortality during follow-up. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to explore nonlinear dose–response relationships, and segmented regression models were used to estimate exploratory turning points. Results Among 564 patients, 212 (37.6%) had elevated hs-cTnT (>14 ng/L). Elevated hs-cTnT was independently associated with poor 90-day mRS (adjusted OR 1.93, 95% CI, 1.22–3.05; p = 0.005) and all-cause mortality during follow-up (fully adjusted HR 4.12, 95% CI, 2.31–7.48; p < 0.001). During a median follow-up of 17 months (IQR 12–26 months), Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower overall survival in patients with elevated hs-cTnT ( p < 0.001). RCS analysis revealed significant nonlinear associations between hs-cTnT and both endpoints ( p < 0.001). Exploratory model-derived turning points were observed at 28.42 ng/L for functional outcome and 31.68 ng/L for mortality; these should be interpreted as exploratory rather than validated clinical cutoffs. Below these values, risk increased more steeply; above them, no statistically significant further increase in risk was observed. Conclusion Admission hs-cTnT was independently associated with 90-day functional outcome and all-cause mortality during follow-up in patients with AIS. The association appeared to be nonlinear, with model-derived turning points at approximately 28–32 ng/L that should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive clinical cutoffs. Clinically, hs-cTnT may be useful as a complementary marker for identifying patients at higher risk who may warrant closer neuro-cardiac evaluation, although its incremental predictive value has not been formally assessed.

title: Prognostic determinants in AECOPD differ by cardiovascular disease status: a two-center retrospective cohort study in China
authors: Xunliang Tong; Tongji Xie; ying Tang; Lan Liu; Peng Yin; Tianyu Li; Donghao Liu; Xiaowei Jiang; Xiaoman Du; Yuan Zhang; Weiwei Cui; Claus F. Vogelmeier; Dan Li; Yanming Li
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) comorbidity is common among patients with acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) and is associated with poor prognosis. However, whether the presence of CVD modifies the prognostic determinants in AECOPD remains unclear, and there is a lack of validated risk stratification tools that account for this heterogeneity, particularly in China. This retrospective cohort study enrolled 1584 patients hospitalized for AECOPD from two centers in China. Patients were classified as CVD or non-CVD based on prespecified cardiovascular conditions. Cause-specific mortality was analyzed using data linked to the National Mortality Surveillance System. The primary outcome was overall survival from index hospitalization (OS1). OS2 (from first symptom onset) was analyzed as an exploratory outcome. Hospitalization duration was modeled using negative binomial regression. The models were developed in the Beijing cohort (70% training/30% internal test) and externally validated in the Jilin cohort. Respiratory-related death was the predominant cause across all subgroups, accounting for approximately half of all deaths. Compared with non-CVD patients, those with CVD had significantly longer hospital stays (8.71 days vs 7.98 days, P < 0.001) and worse long-term survival (3-year OS1 rate: 76.6% vs. 85.4%, P < 0.001). External validation demonstrated moderate discrimination for the CVD model of OS1 ( C-index : 0.700, 95% CI 0.611–0.773) and non-CVD model of OS1 ( C-index : 0.662, 95%CI 0.565–0.744). Sensitivity analysis including hypertension in the CVD definition and filtering early death yielded consistent results. Our findings suggest that prognostic determinants differ substantially between CVD and non-CVD groups, supporting a hypothesis-generating framework for stratified risk assessment. A stratified prognostication framework in which CVD status dictates the use of different risk calculators was built and paved the way for more practical management strategies in China.

title: Circulating osteocrin is associated with cardiac remodeling in canine myxomatous mitral valve disease and skeletal alterations in a rat pressure-overload model
authors: Masafumi Komatsu; Hiromu Udagawa; Ryuji Araki; Yuji Hamamoto; Eunryel Nam; Minoru Okamoto; Mitsuhiro Isaka
abstract: Background Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is the most common acquired cardiac disease in dogs and is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder associated with extracardiac remodeling. Osteocrin (OSTN), a secreted peptide implicated in natriuretic peptide biology and skeletal homeostasis, has emerged as a potential candidate biomarker of cardiovascular–skeletal interactions. However, circulating OSTN dynamics during cardiovascular disease progression remain incompletely characterized. Methods We employed a translational study design integrating a clinical cohort of dogs with naturally occurring myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) and an experimental rat pressure-overload remodeling model. Circulating OSTN concentrations were evaluated alongside cardiac biomarkers, echocardiographic indices, bone mineral density, skeletal mechanical properties, and tissue localization by immunohistochemistry. Results In the canine cohort ( n = 47), circulating OSTN concentrations demonstrated stage-dependent alterations and were significantly associated with echocardiographic indices of cardiac remodeling. In the rat pressure-overload model, circulating OSTN concentrations increased, whereas NT-proBNP did not show a significant pressure-overload-associated increase. In pooled analyses, circulating OSTN was inversely associated with bone mineral density and stiffness; however, these associations were substantially influenced by between-group separation, whereas no significant associations were observed between NT-proBNP and the skeletal parameters examined. Multivariable regression analysis demonstrated that ACVIM disease stage remained significantly associated with circulating OSTN concentrations after adjustment for age and body weight. Conclusion Circulating OSTN was associated with cardiac remodeling in dogs with MMVD and with skeletal alterations in an experimental rat pressure-overload model. These findings support further investigation of OSTN as a candidate biomarker at the interface between cardiovascular and skeletal remodeling.

title: Association of pre-existing cardiovascular disease with cardiovascular and clinical outcomes in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors
authors: Lama Alfehaid; Ahmed S. Alanazi; Mansour Alomran; Hadi Skouri; Nada Alsuhebany
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer therapy but are increasingly associated with cardiovascular complications. The association between pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and cardiovascular outcomes among patients receiving ICIs remains incompletely characterized, particularly in real-world settings. To evaluate the association between baseline CVD and cardiovascular and clinical outcomes among adult patients treated with ICIs. We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study at two tertiary hospitals in Saudi Arabia, including adult patients who received at least one ICI dose between January 2017 and January 2023. Baseline CVD was defined as documented cardiovascular disease before ICI initiation. The primary outcome was a composite of new cardiovascular events occurring after ICI initiation. The secondary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used multivariable logistic regression to identify factors independently associated with cardiovascular events, with sensitivity analyses incorporating additional cardiovascular risk factors. Among 608 patients, 54 (8.9%) had baseline CVD. Patients with baseline CVD were older and had a greater burden of comorbidities than those without baseline CVD. During follow-up, 69 patients (11.3%) experienced at least one cardiovascular event. Cardiovascular events occurred in 27 of 54 patients (50.0%) with baseline CVD compared with 42 of 554 patients (7.6%) without baseline CVD ( p < 0.001). Baseline CVD was independently associated with higher odds of cardiovascular events (adjusted OR, 9.46; 95% CI 4.92–18.17; p < 0.001), and increasing age was also independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR per year, 1.04; 95% CI 1.01–1.06; p = 0.001). The association remained significant after additional adjustment for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and dyslipidemia (adjusted OR, 6.64; 95% CI 3.28–13.47; p < 0.001). All-cause mortality was higher among patients with baseline CVD (64.8% vs. 46.4%, p = 0.010), and unadjusted median overall survival was shorter (11.5 vs. 23.8 months; log-rank p = 0.022). Cardiovascular events were predominantly ischemic and heart failure-related, whereas myocarditis was rare, occurring in only one patient overall. In this multicenter cohort, pre-existing CVD was independently associated with higher cardiovascular event odds among ICI patients, even after adjusting for risk factors. These patients also had shorter OS, though survival analysis was unadjusted. Findings suggest baseline CVD patients are vulnerable and may benefit from thorough risk assessment and cardio-oncology care. However, as an observational study without a non-ICI comparator, these associations do not prove ICI caused or worsened CVD.

title: Antecedents and consequences of Green-tech FDI in emerging markets
authors: Zhuoran Liu
abstract: As environmental pressures intensify, attracting sustainable foreign direct investment (FDI), particularly green-tech FDI, has become a critical pathway for emerging markets to achieve environmental sustainability. However, existing research remains fragmented, offering limited insights into why green-tech FDI enters emerging markets and how it affects regional green innovation. This thesis addresses these gaps by systematically examining both the antecedents and consequences of green-tech FDI through three empirical studies using regional data from China. Study 1 and Study 2 focus on the antecedents of green-tech FDI. Study 1 examines how host-country conditions can attract green-tech FDI, highlighting the role of environmental management information disclosure (EMID) by domestic firms in reducing information gaps and strengthening green market–seeking motives. Study 2 shifts attention to the active decision-making of green-tech FDI, showing that under uncertainty, green-tech foreign investors engage in identity-based bandwagon learning by imitating peers with similar green identities, thereby mitigating investment risks. Study 3 turns to the consequences of green-tech FDI. It demonstrates that, due to the technological complexity of green innovation and limited absorptive capacity in emerging markets, green-tech FDI may generate crowding-out effects rather than purely positive spillovers. Adopting a network perspective, the study further finds that universities play a key moderating role: through broad linkages and deep collaborations, they help mitigate negative spillovers and facilitate the diffusion of green technologies. Together, the three studies advance the literature on sustainable FDI by differentiating green-tech FDI from general FDI and identifying the specific mechanisms that shape its entry decisions and local innovation outcomes. Practically, the findings provide guidance for emerging-market governments and firms on how to attract and manage sustainable investment, balance growth with environmental objectives, and strengthen local innovation ecosystems.

title: Combating Data and Target Shifts in Visual Tasks
authors: Zhaorui Tan
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep learning models for visual tasks has led to significant progress in many domains. However, a key challenge remains: ensuring that models can generalize effectively to unseen samples or novel classes, especially in real-world scenarios where training data-target pairs are often limited or unavailable, and test data may exhibit shifts in both data and targets. This thesis addresses the problem of shifts across data and targets, proposing novel methods to improve model generalization and transferability in complex settings. The thesis identifies the different shift scenarios for visual tasks and presents their problem forms. The research first relaxes the static target distribution assumption in Multi-Domain Generalization (mDG) tasks, introducing the General Multi-Domain Generalization (GMDG) objective to improve generalization under varying data shifts. Specifically, Extensive experiments validate that GMDG is feasible for classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Further considering extreme target distribution shifts where even unknown novel classes emerge, the study also explores logical regularization techniques for tasks such as Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), mDG+GCD, and Class Incremental Learning (CIL), proposing a sample-based logical regularization term (L-Reg) to enhance data-, target-, and all-shift generalization. Additionally, a partial logic framework is introduced to address challenges in CIL, enabling models to retain room for unknown classes during training. This is further extended by the Partial-Logic Regularization (PL-Reg), which improves generalization across GCD, mDG+GCD, and transferability for CIL tasks. Furthermore, the thesis proposes a novel Semantic-aware Data Augmentation (SADA) framework for cross-modality generalization in text-to-image synthesis (T2Isyn), text-image retrieval (TIR), and image-text retrieval (ITR) tasks. This framework ensures semantic preservation across text and image modalities, improving both semantic consistency and image quality in cross-modality tasks. The methods proposed in this thesis offer significant advancements in visual generalization and transfer scenarios, providing theoretical insights and practical solutions for handling data shifts, target shifts, and multi-modalities in complex scenarios. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating their superior performance across a range of tasks.

title: Depth of Processing, learner aptitude, and the acquisition of L2 English grammatical structures
authors: Shweta Nigam
abstract: Depth of Processing (DoP) is central to several models of instructed second language acquisition (ISLA) (Leow, 2015). While DoP has been extensively examined in vocabulary learning (e.g., Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001), its role in the acquisition of grammatical structures, particularly through oral and audio-visual modalities remains comparatively underexplored. Drawing on the Levels of Processing framework (Craik & Lockhart, 1972), this study investigated whether task-induced processing depth influences the acquisition of third conditionals and comparatives, and whether language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) predicts learning gains. Using a pretest–posttest design, four intact classes involving 108 Grade 8 EFL learners in India were assigned to one of the three experimental conditions differing in level and type of processing: Low DoP, High DoP Explicit, and High DoP Implicit. The treatment task required the participants to listen to an audio-visual story containing the target structures (third conditionals and comparatives) and complete analytic tasks (varying in different groups) before listening to the story for a second time. The oral performance of the participants was analysed for accuracy, and frequency of use of the target structures. A grammaticality judgement test (GJT) and an elicited imitation task (EIT) were used to assess the participants’ gains in the knowledge of the target structures. In addition, language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) was measured and modelled as a predictor of gain scores. Results showed a significant effect of processing condition on GJT performance with the High DoP Implicit group outperforming the High DoP Explicit group on total scores and comparatives. In contrast, ANCOVA analyses indicated no significant group differences on EIT outcomes once pretest performance was controlled, with pretest scores strongly predicting posttest performance. In oral production, processing effects were structure-specific: the Low DoP group showed greater accuracy gains for comparatives, while both High DoP groups revealed increased frequency of use of third conditionals. However, across all four measures, multiple regression analyses indicated that LLAMA B, D, and F did not significantly predict gain scores. Overall, the findings support a processing-by-structure pattern: deeper processing benefits were most evident for the more salient structure (comparatives) on an explicit, written measure, whereas complex, low-salience forms (third conditionals) showed limited accuracy change but increased frequency of use under deeper processing.

title: A UAV-Based Framework for Community-Scale Residential Building Energy Modelling in China
authors: Mengfan Jin
abstract: With increasing emphasis on energy efficiency and carbon emission reduction in the building sector, rapid and scalable energy modelling of existing buildings is critical for retrofit projects and policy development. Conventional surveys, data collection and energy modelling processes remain labour-intensive and impractical for large-scale applications, and energy modelling often dominates project time and cost. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with high-resolution and infrared cameras now offer fast and safe exterior surveys, showing great potential in building energy assessments. Yet, a systematic framework for UAV integration, from image capture through processing to inputs for building energy simulation, has not been established. This research addresses these challenges by developing a structured framework for community-scale building energy modelling, which integrates UAV photogrammetry to accelerate data acquisition, reduce labour, and shorten energy modelling time for retrofit projects. The framework is designed to minimise prior data requirements while maximising automation and retaining sufficient accuracy and reliability. It also addressed systemic issues, such as the lack of data necessary to fully exploit the potential of available technologies in the context of this study. To achieve this research objective, a mixed-methodology approach, combining desk studies and fieldwork, was adopted. First, a comprehensive review of UAV-based building energy studies mapped the current applications and available tools, proposing a preliminary framework. Fieldwork then encompassed a pilot study and a detailed case study. In the pilot test, a single building was surveyed to identify an optimal toolchain for flight planning, image capture, photogrammetric reconstruction, model generation, and selection of a simulation platform. The resulting refined framework was applied to a case study of a 39-building community, and it was demonstrated that further automation was necessary. The potential for automation was then further explored. Geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning techniques were compared, and the combination that best balanced accuracy and processing time was selected for 3D model generation and window-to-wall ratio (WWR) extraction. In parallel, an archetype library of residential buildings in the Hot Summer Cold Winter (HSCW) zone in China was compiled to facilitate the assignment of thermal parameters. Finally, a reusable community-scale building energy modelling (CBEM) workflow was assembled in Grasshopper using Ladybug Tools components to process the aforementioned inputs. In conclusion, this study integrates UAV photogrammetry, GIS-based geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and graphical programming to develop an UAV-CBEM framework. The outcomes establish a foundation for scalable UAV-based building energy assessments, enhancing applicability in data-limited and large-scale settings worldwide.

title: Spectral Materialism: Encounters with land-time-scapes
authors: Nightingale, Sam
abstract: This transdisciplinary, practice-based PhD introduces spectral materialism through art-based research encounters with ecologically and historically stratified land-time-scapes shaped by hypersalinity and colonial terraforming. Centred in the semi-arid Mallee (southeastern Australia) and read through echoes with California’s Imperial Valley, the project examines how spectral time—the co-presence and haunting of other temporalities—manifests in the material conditions of salt, soil, water, plants, and infrastructures. It asks how learning from geological, First Nations, colonial, and ecological pasts can orient responsibilities in unsettled futures. Treating the present as a crisis of time as much as a crisis of matter, the thesis critiques linear-progressive temporalities bound to Western modernity and extractive regimes. In response, spectral materialism is developed as both a conceptual framework and a critical creative methodology. Through alchemical media experiments with salt crystals, hypersaline soils, and halophytes, photography is reconfigured as a site-responsive, process-oriented practice. Salt is engaged as a material agent and ‘time-crystal’ whose phase shifts—dissolution, saturation, precipitation, crystallisation, evaporation—form a meta-chemistry that refracts deep-marine pasts, settler-colonial irrigation infrastructures, and contemporary dust into processual renderings of time. Methodologically, the project advances attunement as a mode of sensing and responsiveness to forces that are not always immediately perceptible yet are materially active. Field notes appear as para-writing, interrupting linear narration so that heterogeneous times co-present themselves within the text. The thesis is guided by First Nations temporalities—time as relational and in place—while remaining accountable to ethical limits and protocols. The contribution is twofold: a theoretical articulation of spectral materialism as a way to think time otherwise, and a set of site-responsive methods for engaging elemental media in saline environments. Together, they generate materially grounded accounts of spectral presences and open alternative pathways for knowing, sensing, and relating within land-time-scapes marked by enduring colonial and ecological afterlives amid planetary change.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND COMMERCIALIZATION OF COMPUTATIONAL METHODS TO ACCELERATE DERMATOLOGICAL DISCOVERY
authors: Jasson Makkar
abstract: The skin is the largest and outermost organ that surrounds the human body and provides a physical barrier that protects the more delicate internal tissues from the harsh surrounding environment. Over the course of evolution, specialized structures have also arisen in the skin, including sweat and sebaceous glands, nails and claws, and hair follicles. The hair follicle is a multi-lineage mini-organ that is a critical component in defining mammalian species. The gain of function derived from hair and fur benefited these species for millennia due to its insulative and protective properties, mechanosensing function, and ability to serve as camouflage. Current approaches to assess these fibers are generally non-quantitative or are low throughput due to technical limitations of ‘splitting hairs’. We developed a novel deep learning-based computer vision approach for the high throughput quantification of individual hair fibers at a high resolution. Our innovative computer vision tool can distinguish and extract overlapping fibers for quantification of multivariate features including length, width, and color to generate single-hair phenomes (shPhenome) of diverse conditions across the lifespan of mice. Using our tool, we explored the effects of hormone signaling, genetic modifications, and aging on hair follicle output. These analyses revealed novel hair phenotypes as a result of endocrinological, developmental, and aging-related alterations in the fur coats of mice. This tool was then adapted to capture more nuanced hair phenotypes, such as curvature, in a variety of mouse models harboring genetic perturbations. Commercialization of the deep hair phenomics technology presented a unique opportunity to pursue research translation, transforming fundamental biological research into marketable products. Much like the traditional academic route, the path to commercialization requires consistent and continuous iteration, testing of hypotheses, and allowing data to influence and lead subsequent actions. However, as opposed to the pursuit of knowledge, translating research into market-ready solutions requires a focus on consumer needs and the identification of market opportunities. Additionally, the shift in incentive structure requires commercial ventures to prioritize intellectual property protection, alter capital and resource allocation, and seek alternative fundraising sources. The entrepreneurial foundation built through this process culminated in the filing of a provisional patent and establishment of a startup company, kerat Inc. This journey illuminated the multifaceted challenges inherent in closing the gap between academic innovation and commercially viable goods, requiring simultaneous advancement of technical capabilities, adaptation to market dynamics, and fabrication of business infrastructure. Overall, the culmination of work presented in this dissertation sheds light on the importance of quantitatively assessing hair fiber properties to capture the biological phenomena that underlie this fundamental feature of mammalian skin. These findings also highlight the capabilities of this methodology for identifying perturbations in normal growth, potentially indicative of disease or dysfunction. Lastly, this showcased the potential of this technology’s commercial use cases in both the cosmetics and diagnostics industries.
